newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sectarian link seen in Pakistan policeman's murder.
newsitem.headline: Sectarian link seen in Pakistan policeman's murder.

text.p: Gunmen killed a senior police officer in the Pakistani city of Gujranwala on Tuesday in what police said might have been revenge for his work in tracking down Sunni Moslem militants.
They said the unidentified attackers ambushed senior police superintendent Mohammad Ashraf Marth on his way to work in an official vehicle at about 8.45 a.m. (0345 GMT).
Marth, 35, died on the spot along with his driver, Mohammad Tabassum. The assailants escaped in a car, police said.

Police sources said the attack was likely to have been linked to Marth's arrest of six Sunni militants in connection with a February assault on the Iranian cultural centre in the Punjab city of Multan, where he was then posted.
Eight people, including the centre's Iranian director, were killed in the Multan attack, believed to be the work of a militant anti-Shi'ite group known as Lashkar-i-Jhangvi.

Police said Marth had been threatened after the arrests and warned to proceed no further. He was transferred to Gujranwala, also in Punjab, while the six Sunni militants remain in jail awaiting trial.
Marth is related to members of a leading political family in the province, including Punjab provincial assembly speaker Pervaiz Ellahi and Federal Interior Minister Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain.
His killing happened amid a surge in sectarian violence ahead of the start on Friday of the Shi'ite Moslem mourning month of Muharram, when religious tension often runs high.
Two Shi'ite activists were shot dead on Monday, one in the Punjab capital Lahore and the other in the city of Faisalabad, bringing this year's sectarian death toll to about 70.

Most of the violence, involving tit-for-tat attacks by Sunni and Shi'ite militants, has taken place in populous Punjab province, where troops have been ordered to stand by to help civil authorities during Muharram.
Leaders of Sunni and Shi'ite religious parties, including several militant groups, met Punjab government officials on Monday and pledged to keep the peace during Muharram.

They agreed to a seven-point code of conduct to honour each other's beliefs, avoid criticism of other sects, preach unity and religious harmony, and to tolerate processions and religious activities during Muharram.
The parties also pledged to help the administration and peace committees maintain law and order.
Participants included Azam Tariq, leader of the militant Sunni Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan group, and Allama Munawer, chief of the rival Shi'ite Sipah-i-Muhammad Pakistan faction.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and his brother Shahbaz Sharif, who is chief minister of Punjab province, have sworn to stamp out sectarian violence, which has emerged as the main security challenge to his government since it took power in February.
Shi'ites make up an estimated 15 percent of Pakistan's mainly Sunni population of about 138 million.
